tips.title: Le premier, then plain numbers
tips.body: Only the first of the month is an ordinal: **le premier janvier**. Every other date is a plain number: *le deux février*, *le vingt-cinq décembre*. Never *le deuxième février*.

tips.title: On takes the il form
tips.body: *On* is grammatically singular, so *on **mange***, *on **est***, *on **va***. Writing *on mangent* is a frequent and easily avoided error.

tips.title: A superlative needs the article twice
tips.body: *La fête **la plus** animée*: the article appears before the noun and again before *plus*. Leaving out the second one is the usual slip.

tips.title: Only the first is ordinal
tips.body: Dates need **le premier** for the 1st and then plain numbers for everything else: *le deux janvier*, *le quinze août*. One exception, learnt once, and every other date in the topic follows the same simple pattern without thinking.

steps.title: Les fêtes
steps.body:
Festivals are a **culture** topic as well as a language one: It helps to know something about how French-speaking people celebrate. The vocabulary first, then the calendar.

*Une fête* is a festival, a holiday, or a party, depending on context; *fêter* or *célébrer* is *to celebrate*. *Un jour férié* is a public holiday, when shops close.

steps.title: The French year
steps.body:
The festivals that come up in reading and listening texts, in calendar order. A few are French versions of celebrations you know; others, like *la fête de la musique* and *la Chandeleur*, are their own thing.

- **6 January, l'Épiphanie**: *la galette des rois*, with *la fève* hidden inside. Whoever finds it is king or queen for the day.
- **2 February, la Chandeleur**: everyone makes *crêpes*.
- **February, le carnaval**: *Nice* has the most famous, with floats and people in costume.
- **1 April, le poisson d'avril**: tricks, and paper fish stuck on backs.
- **1 May, la fête du Travail**: people give sprigs of *muguet* for luck.
- **21 June, la fête de la musique**: free concerts in the streets, since 1982.
- **14 July, la fête nationale**: the military *défilé* on the Champs-Élysées, fireworks, and the *bal des pompiers*.
- **24 to 25 December, Noël**: *le réveillon* on Christmas Eve, *la bûche de Noël*, presents under *le sapin*.
- **31 December, la Saint-Sylvestre**: New Year's Eve, with another *réveillon*.

Many French families also celebrate *l'Aïd*, *Hanoukka* or *Diwali*; a reading text may describe any of them.

steps.title: Dates, and on for what people do
steps.body:
Two pieces of grammar do most of the work in this topic.

**Dates** are *le* + number + month, with no *of*: *le quatorze juillet*, *le vingt-et-un juin*. The only ordinal is the first: **le premier janvier**, *le premier mai*. Months have no capital letter.

**On** is the pronoun for customs: what people do in general. It takes the *il* form of the verb: *on mange des crêpes*, *on offre du muguet*, *on se déguise*, *on regarde le défilé*. In English it comes out as *we*, *people* or *you*. It saves you from *les gens font* every time, and examiners like it.

steps.title: The biggest, the best, the most important
steps.body:
Comparing festivals needs the **superlative**, and it needs one rule you met last half term: the adjective keeps its usual place.

- After the noun, repeat the article: *la fête **la plus** importante*, *le festival **le plus** connu*.
- Before the noun (*grand, petit, beau*): *le plus grand carnaval*, *la plus belle fête*.
- **Le meilleur / la meilleure** for *the best*: *la meilleure fête de l'année*.

And the comparative for a contrast: *le 14 juillet est plus animé que Noël*; *Noël est plus familial que le Nouvel An*.

A superlative with an opinion and a reason is a top-band sentence: *pour moi, la fête de la musique est la meilleure fête de l'année parce que tout le monde participe*.

steps.title: Describing a festival
steps.body: A description in the present: what it is, when, what people do, and what you think. *On* carries the customs, *il y a* carries the scene.

steps.text: *Le 14 juillet, c'est la fête nationale en France.*
*Le matin, il y a un grand défilé militaire sur les Champs-Élysées.*
steps.note: il y a for the scene

steps.text: *Le soir, on regarde le feu d'artifice et on danse au bal des pompiers.*
*C'est un jour férié, donc tout le monde est en vacances.*
*À mon avis, c'est la fête la plus animée de l'année.*

steps.title: A festival you went to
steps.body:
The writing and speaking tasks usually add *a time you celebrated*: one occasion, so the **perfect** for what you did and the **imperfect** for what it was like — the same pair as the holiday story.

*L'année dernière, je suis allé au carnaval de Nice avec ma classe. Il y avait beaucoup de monde, les chars étaient énormes et tout le monde était déguisé. Nous avons dansé dans les rues et c'était vraiment magnifique.*

Useful scene-setters, all imperfect: **il y avait beaucoup de monde** (there were a lot of people), **c'était animé** (it was lively), **il y avait de l'ambiance** (there was a great atmosphere), **tout le monde était…** (everyone was…).

steps.title: Going deeper: culture questions, and opinions on tradition
steps.body:
**Know the facts, and use them.** A reading text will assume you know that *la fête de la musique* is free and on 21 June, or that *la galette* hides a *fève*. In writing, one accurate cultural detail — *le bal des pompiers*, *le muguet du 1er mai* — gives you something concrete and specific to say.

**Discuss traditions, both ways.** The top-band question is often *are traditions important?* Have a sentence each way: *les traditions sont importantes parce qu'elles rassemblent les familles*; *mais certaines fêtes sont devenues trop commerciales*. Then judge: *même si*, *cependant*, *à mon avis*.

**Read the small words.** *Gratuit*, *chaque année*, *avoir lieu*, *même si*, *depuis 1982*: comprehension questions turn on them.

**Pronouns.** *Je les ai regardés* (I watched them): the object pronoun before the auxiliary, with the participle agreeing. Not required for the mark, but it is what a grade 9 script looks like.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Vocabulary**: *fêter*, *un jour férié*, *le défilé*, *le feu d'artifice*, *se déguiser*, *offrir*, *le réveillon*, *gratuit*.
- **The calendar**: Épiphanie 6 janvier (galette, fève) · Chandeleur 2 février (crêpes) · carnaval (Nice) · poisson d'avril · 1er mai (muguet) · fête de la musique 21 juin (free) · 14 juillet (défilé, feu d'artifice, bal) · Noël (réveillon, bûche) · Saint-Sylvestre.
- **Dates**: *le* + number + month; only *le premier* is ordinal.
- **On** for customs, with the *il* form: *on mange, on offre, on se déguise*.
- **Superlatives**: *la fête la plus importante*, *le plus grand carnaval*, *la meilleure fête*.
- **One occasion**: perfect for what you did, imperfect for the scene (*il y avait beaucoup de monde*).
- **Traditions**: an opinion each way, then a judgement with *même si*.

examTechnique.body:
Festivals carry cultural content that Edexcel expects you to recognise: the dates and traditions of the French calendar turn up in listening and reading texts, and an accurate detail in your own writing gives you specific detail to write about. The grammar is light but exact: dates with le and only premier as an ordinal, on with the il form for customs, and the superlative with its repeated article.

When a task asks for a time you celebrated, switch to the perfect for what you did and the imperfect for the scene, exactly as in a holiday account. When it asks whether traditions matter, give a reason for and a reason against, and finish with a judgement.
examinerErrors: *Le un janvier* or *le deuxième février*: only the first of the month is ordinal.
*On mangent* or *on sommes*: *on* takes the *il* form.
*La plus importante fête*: adjectives that follow the noun keep following it, with the article repeated.
Writing *Juillet* or *Décembre* with a capital letter.
Confusing *la fête de la musique* (21 June, free concerts) with *la fête nationale* (14 July).
Giving only one side on whether traditions matter, when the question invites a balanced answer.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer names a festival with its correct date and an accurate tradition, describes the customs with on, compares festivals with a superlative, and narrates one occasion in the perfect with the scene in the imperfect. On traditions it argues both ways and judges, with même si or cependant, and it reads comprehension texts for the small words that carry the meaning.
